name: Sputnik 1
outcome: First artificial satellite; began the space age.
intro: Launched by the Soviet Union on 4 October 1957, Sputnik 1 was a 58 cm aluminum sphere that did little more than orbit Earth and emit a steady radio beep — but that beep, picked up by amateur radio operators worldwide, opened the Space Age and triggered the Space Race. It orbited for three months before burning up in the atmosphere in January 1958.

name: Explorer 1
outcome: First U.S. satellite; discovered the Van Allen radiation belts.
intro: The United States' answer to Sputnik, Explorer 1 reached orbit on 31 January 1958 after a failed first attempt months earlier. Its cosmic-ray detector, built by James Van Allen's team, returned data showing far fewer particles than expected — the instrument had actually saturated from an intense radiation belt, leading to the discovery of what's now called the Van Allen radiation belts.

name: Luna 1
outcome: First spacecraft to pass near the Moon.

name: Luna 2
outcome: First human-made object to reach the Moon.
intro: Luna 2 became the first spacecraft to reach another celestial body when it crash-landed on the Moon in September 1959, ending the mission by design. Along the way it confirmed the Moon has no significant magnetic field, and it scattered Soviet pennants across the lunar surface on impact.

name: Luna 3
outcome: Returned the first images of the lunar far side.
intro: A month after Luna 2, Luna 3 swung around the Moon and photographed its far side for the first time in human history — a hemisphere no one had ever seen, since the Moon is tidally locked to Earth. The grainy images, radioed back and later refined, let Soviet scientists start naming lunar features before anyone else got the chance.

name: Vostok 1
outcome: Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space and in orbit.
intro: On 12 April 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, completing a single orbit of Earth aboard Vostok 1 in 108 minutes. He ejected and parachuted separately from the capsule during descent, per Soviet spacecraft design at the time, though this detail was concealed for years to satisfy record-keeping rules requiring the pilot land with the craft.
